chapter_theme: Under the heading கல்வி, with the payiram and the invocation, ten verses on learning: it must be had in youth, the learner feels his ignorance grow, learning that does not clear confusion is worthless, the learned are at home everywhere, hearing excels solitary study, a young Chola judges by inherited craft, only the learned or the better can judge learning and goodness, the learned are restrained, and their faults are seen by all.

payiram.reading: The prefatory verse says that the king of Munrurai, bowing at the feet of the Lord who sits in the shade of the pindi tree, made all four hundred old proverbs into four-line venpas and set them out sweetly.
payiram.nuance: The pindi (asoka) tree is the tree under which the Jain Arhat is shown seated, so the bow places the work in a Jain frame without naming the faith. The proverbs are called பண்டை, already old: the poet claims to have set them in verse, not to have made them, and names himself only by his seat, முன்றுறை மன்னவன்.

0.reading: The invocation sets the feet of the one who quelled the enemy within and knew without flaw beside the rising of those in the wide sea-girt world who have seen and known them as their due, and clinches it with the proverb that the steam of a great thing is great.
0.nuance: The sentence has no main verb: the feet stand at the head and the worshippers' rise is compared to something left unsaid, so the sense is carried by the proverb, that what issues from a great thing is itself great, here the standing that comes to those who know the great one's feet. அரி may be the senses' enemies or delusion; ஆசின்று உணர்ந்தவன் reads as one who knows without fault, an epithet of the omniscient one.

pazhamozhi.literal: the steam (or breath) of a great thing is great

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the greatness that passes from the worshipped one to those who know his feet

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who know the great one's feet rise high in turn

1.reading: The verse asks whether one who would not learn in the youth that is fit for it can expect to gain learning in old age, and answers with the proverb that no one ever took toll after the wilderness road was passed, nor wages after the tree was cleared.
1.nuance: Both halves of the proverb are about payment that can only be taken while the work is still to be done: once the road is crossed or the tree is moved, the claim is gone. Youth is cast as that moment for learning. மரம்போக்கி may be the felling of a tree or the plying of a boat (மரம், a raft) across water; either way the wage falls due before the task ends.

pazhamozhi.proverb: சுரம்போக்கி உல்குகொண்டார் இல்லையே யில்லை மரம்போக்கிக் கூலிகொண் டார்
pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who took toll after the desert road was crossed, none who took wages after the tree was cleared

story.act: no story; the proverb is the instance, a payment that lapses once the work is past

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learning not gained in youth cannot be claimed in old age

2.reading: Because a man lapses at every word he speaks, the one who, without flagging, laments at each stage of study that he has not yet learnt, ponders one thing and labours until he knows it, knows the truth of the saying that the more one learns the more one finds oneself unlearned.
2.nuance: The verse makes the sense of one's own ignorance a working method, not a mood: the lament drives the next round of pondering and labour (உற்றொன்று சிந்தித்து உழன்றொன்று அறியுமேல்). The first line gives the reason as the lapses that each spoken word exposes. The grammar of lines 1 to 3 is loose and the subject is supplied.

pazhamozhi.literal: how, with each learning, one is the more unlearned

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the earnest learner who measures himself after each lesson

pazhamozhi.applied_to: true study shows the learner how much remains unlearnt

3.reading: A lamp is bought for a price only after everything is weighed to be sure it will not flicker, and if the lamp itself should spread confusion, lord of the hill country, what use is it, for no one pays money to buy darkness.
3.nuance: The verse never names learning: the lamp stands for it only through the heading, and the point is that knowledge bought at a cost is worth having only if it clears confusion (மருள்). One may also read it as advice to test a teacher or a text before taking it, as one tests a lamp before paying.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one gives wealth to buy darkness

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the purchase of a lamp that gives no light

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learning that leaves one confused is worth nothing for its cost

4.reading: Those who have learnt deeply are the wise, and there is no land in the four directions they do not go to; those lands are not foreign to them but their own, so, as the proverb says, they need no food for the road.
4.nuance: The proverb turns belonging into provision: the learned carry nothing because every land feeds them as its own. Line 1 as printed (ஆற்றவும் கற்றவும்) is awkward; the reading takes it as 'those who have learnt much'.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no need of food for the journey

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned traveller

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned are at home everywhere and need nothing carried

5.reading: The wise do not become like the frog in the well that thinks there is no sweet water to drink anywhere else, and even beside reciting a treatise sweetly all day without tiring, the proverb holds that hearing is better than learning.
5.nuance: The frog image gives the reason for the ranking: one's own text, however diligently recited, is one well, and hearing from others is what shows there is water elsewhere. So the verse ranks listening above solitary study, not above learning as such. கணக்கு is the treatise or text conned by rote.

story.act: the frog in the well takes its well for the only sweet water there is

pazhamozhi.applied_to: listening to others frees the learner from the narrowness of his own text

6.reading: When grey-haired elders said a young man could not see a case through to its end, the Chola tied on grey hair, judged the case by his words to their satisfaction, and so proved the saying that a family's craft is half known without being learnt.
6.nuance: The proverb credits the king's skill to birth, not study: his line's craft of judging comes to him half-made. That sits oddly under a heading on learning, and against the counted works that rank learning above lineage. The disguise answers the elders on their own terms, appearance, while the judgement answers them on substance.

pazhamozhi.literal: a family's craft is half-known without being learnt

story.act: a young Chola king, doubted by grey elders, put on grey hair and judged their case to their satisfaction
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Karikalan; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: inherited capacity: the king judges well though young

7.reading: Only the deeply learned can discern the scholarship of the deeply learned, lord of the town of flowering waters; it is not open to common people, for a snake knows the feet of a snake.
7.nuance: The proverb rests on the belief that a snake's legs are hidden from all but other snakes: learning is not merely hard for outsiders to judge, it is invisible to them.

pazhamozhi.literal: a snake knows a snake's feet

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned judging the learned

pazhamozhi.applied_to: only peers in learning can judge learning

8.reading: If the goodness of the good is to be known, those better than they will know it and others will not, lord of the great hill where peacocks dance, for spear is split only by spear.
8.nuance: The verse is about goodness of character, not learning, though it stands under the learning heading; it pairs with 7 but asks more, since the knower must be better (அவரினும் நல்லார), not merely equal. அயில் is a spear point or iron: a hard thing is cut only by what is as hard or harder.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the judging of goodness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: only those better than the good can know their goodness

9.reading: Those who do not know the restraint that the widely learned have found praise themselves in their heedlessness, lord of the fair hill country where the falls strike the rock, for a full pot does not slop its water.
9.nuance: Self-praise is traced to two lacks at once: not knowing the learned man's restraint, and பொச்சாப்பு, forgetful heedlessness. The proverb implies the half-filled pot without saying it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a full pot does not slop its water

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the quiet of the truly learned against the boasting of the shallow

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned are restrained, the half-learned boast

10.reading: When those who have learnt the prescribed texts and live conspicuously in their town go beyond the texts of those who teach and do blameworthy things, it is a spot fallen on the face of the moon.
10.nuance: The fault is no larger in the learned, but more visible, because they are seen across the town as the moon is seen across the sky. Lines 1 and 2 are hard: வேற்றுமை இல்லார் may mean those of steady conduct or those without distinction of rank, and கதிப்பவர் may be those who expound or the revered; the reading takes the general sense.

pazhamozhi.literal: a blemish fallen on the surface of the moon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the misdeed of a learned and well-known man

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the faults of the learned are seen by all

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 92 lists not learning in youth as one of four faults; Pazhamozhi 1 says why it is a fault: the chance does not return in old age.
links.teaches: The counted verse names the fault and moves on; the proverb supplies its logic, that learning is a toll only collectable while the road is still ahead.

links.note: Naladiyar 135 says learners have few days and so must choose what to learn; Pazhamozhi 1 locates those days in youth and says that once past they cannot be used at all.
links.teaches: Together they make two limits on learning, a short life that forces choice and a closing season of youth after which no choice remains.
links.list_adds: its proverb of toll and wages turns the quatrain's shortness of days into a deadline, a payment that lapses once the work is past.

links.note: Kural 1110 uses the learner's growing sense of ignorance as a simile for love; Pazhamozhi 2 states the same thing of learning itself and makes it the engine of study.
links.teaches: The Kural borrows from learning a fact Pazhamozhi takes as a method: the lament 'I have not learnt' drives the next round of pondering and labour.
links.list_adds: it gives the simile's base in its own right and adds the practice it drives, reflection on one thing at a time, which the love couplet has no room for.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 28 says that as one learns ignorance lessens, step by step toward truth; Pazhamozhi 2 says the earnest learner finds himself the more unlearned at each step.
links.teaches: Read together, ignorance shrinks in fact while the learner's sense of it grows, so the Nanmanikkadigai's ladder is climbed only by one who feels farther from the top.

links.note: Naladiyar 140 says worldly learning without the books of wisdom is clamour that removes no confusion; Pazhamozhi 3 compares learning that leaves confusion to a lamp bought that gives darkness.
links.teaches: The quatrain says which learning fails to clear confusion; the proverb adds the cost, that such learning is a price paid for darkness.
links.list_adds: its lamp-buying image frames learning as a purchase to be tested before paying, which the quatrain's judgement of book against book does not.

links.note: Kural 397 says every land and town is the learned man's own; Pazhamozhi 4 says the same and closes with the proverb that he needs no food for the road.
links.teaches: The Kural states belonging and asks why anyone stays unlearned; Pazhamozhi turns belonging into maintenance, the learned eat wherever they go.
links.list_adds: the proverb carries the couplet's claim of belonging into the traveller's practical case, provision for the journey.

links.note: Kural 414 offers listening to one who has not studied, the ஆயினும் keeping study first; Pazhamozhi 5 says outright that hearing is better than learning.
links.teaches: The two rank the same pair in opposite order: the Kural makes hearing the fallback for the unlearned, Pazhamozhi makes it the cure for the learned man's narrowness.
links.list_adds: its frog-in-the-well image gives a reason for ranking hearing above study, that one's own text is a single well, which the couplet lacks.

links.note: Kural 411 ranks the wealth of the ear first among all wealth; Pazhamozhi 5 ranks hearing above learning itself.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks hearing against wealth, Pazhamozhi against study, so together they set listening at the head of both outer and inner goods.
links.list_adds: it moves the ranking from wealth to learning and names what hearing cures, the well-frog's belief that its own water is the only water.

links.note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to belittle him as young; Pazhamozhi 6 shows elders doing just that and the young Chola answering them.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the rule to the courtier; the story shows the king's side, meeting contempt for his youth with a disguise and a sound judgement.
links.list_adds: it supplies the episode and the cause of the king's competence, his family's craft, which the courtier's rule leaves unstated.

links.note: Naladiyar 195 says austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Pazhamozhi 6 says a lineage gives half its craft without learning.
links.teaches: The pair disagree on which way the gift runs: for the Naladiyar learning makes the family, for Pazhamozhi the family half-supplies the learning.
links.list_adds: its named royal story stakes the claim for inherited capacity on a king's judgement, against the quatrain's denial that birth names anything.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 64 says the world passes over the elder who grew old unlearned and praises the young one who learned; Pazhamozhi 6 also has a young man outdo his elders, but by birth, not study.
links.teaches: Both set the able young against the doubting old, but the counted work credits learning and Pazhamozhi credits lineage, so youth's claim rests on two different grounds.

links.note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those able to examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 7 says it is visible only to the very learned and closed to common people.
links.teaches: The Kural names the audience where learning shines; Pazhamozhi adds that outside it learning is not dimmer but unseen, as a snake's feet are hidden from all but snakes.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes judgement of learning a matter of kind knowing kind, and shuts out the common people the couplet does not mention.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 7 says only the learned know the learned; 8 says the goodness of the good is known only by those better than they.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the claim tightens from peer to superior: learning can be judged by equals, but goodness only by one who exceeds it.

links.note: Naladiyar 256 says the learned keep silent for fear of a lapse while others chatter, like green and dry palm leaves; Pazhamozhi 9 says those ignorant of the learned man's restraint praise themselves, like a pot that is not full.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the learned man's motive for silence; Pazhamozhi names what the noisy lack, knowledge of that restraint and attention to themselves, so the two halves of the contrast each get a cause.
links.list_adds: it narrows the others' chatter to self-praise and traces it to heedlessness, which the leaf image leaves unexplained.

links.note: Kural 978 says greatness bows while smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; Pazhamozhi 9 ties self-praise to not knowing the restraint of the learned.
links.teaches: The Kural sets self-admiration against greatness as a trait; Pazhamozhi makes it a symptom of shallow learning, so boasting becomes evidence of what one has not learnt.
links.list_adds: it moves the claim from greatness in general to learning and gives the full-pot proof that the deeply filled make no noise.

links.note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 10 uses the same image for the misdeed of a learned man known in his town.
links.teaches: The image of the moon's spot passes from birth to learning, so the two together make visibility of fault the cost of any eminence, inherited or earned.
links.list_adds: it carries the couplet's image from lineage to the learned who live conspicuously, and makes their breach of their own texts the fault seen.

new_concepts.gloss: the old saying, the proverb used as the proof that closes a counsel
new_concepts.label_source: the payiram names the work's verses so (பண்டைப் பழமொழி நானூறும்)

source_issues: 4 line 1: ஆற்றவும் கற்றவும் is awkward and may be a corruption of ஆற்றவும் கற்றார்.
0: the invocation lacks a main verb and its first line (அரிதவித்து ஆசின்று) is obscure.
10 lines 1-2: வேற்றுமை இல்லார் and கதிப்பவர் are of uncertain sense.
